meta.notes: All 13 emails in window were read in full via get_thread. None skipped. Charts are not embedded in plaintext bodies; chart counts reflect charts mentioned in text.

items.title: Hottest PPI since 2023 (+1.3% m/m, 6.3% y/y) and the dollar fell anyway
items.idea: Sept PPI +1.3% m/m / 6.3% y/y, core CPI 0.3% vs 0.2% exp. Dollar index touched ~103.00 Wednesday, closed ~101.8 (-0.5% wk). 10y -15bp to 5.09%, 30y -17bp to 5.43%, gold flat (-0.18%). Dauber: the haven was duration, not dollars or gold, and the bid is growth fear, not a Fed pivot.
items.angle: A hot print that fails to lift the dollar is a regime tell. If USD is not the haven, the funding-stress story is about collateral and credit, not rates.
items.tweetA: PPI +1.3% m/m, the hottest since early 2023. Dollar sold off inside two sessions. Gold did nothing. When inflation surprises up and neither USD nor gold catches a bid, the market is not hedging inflation. It is hedging a financing accident.
items.tweetB: Three havens, one winner. Treasuries rallied 15bp on the worst PPI in 3.5 years, USD fell, gold flat. The bond market is pricing a growth scare that the front end refuses to believe. One of them is wrong by December.

items.title: The curve is saying two things: 2y at 4.74% prices a hike, 30y at 5.43% prices a slowdown
items.idea: 2y 4.74% (-6bp), 10y 5.09% (-15bp), 30y 5.43% (-17bp); 2s10s flattened to +35bp from +44bp. Dauber: front end reads inflation, long end reads growth, both cannot be right for long. Call: fade the long-end rally until the 27-28 Oct FOMC. He is wrong if the 30y closes above 5.60% without the 2y moving with it.
items.angle: Falsifiable trade with a stop level: 30y 5.60%. Cross-check with Citi supply news (Treasury may trim 20/30y auctions) which is a competing explanation for the long-end bid.
items.tweetA: Dauber fades the long-end rally into FOMC. The level that proves him wrong is 30y above 5.60% with the 2y not following. I would add a second invalidation: a Nov 4 refunding that cuts 20/30y supply. Technical fade versus structural bid.
items.tweetB: Bull-flattening in a week where the Fed repriced toward a hike. Either the front end is wrong, or the long end is. 2y at 4.74% and 30y at 5.43% are a 69bp bet against each other.

items.title: Brent $109.86, USO +9.15% on the week, natgas -3.18%: oil prices a shock, gas does not
items.idea: Brent settled 109.86, USO +9.15% wk, UNG fund -3.18% (10.66). Energy sector +4.47%, staples +5.37%, tech -7.16%, semis -10.53%. Dauber calls the oil-vs-gas gap the most interesting cross-asset fact of the week.
items.angle: If Hormuz is the driver, why is gas not confirming? Either the oil move is a refined-product/transit story or gas has its own supply cushion. Long energy and staples versus tech is Dauber's explicit pair.
items.tweetA: Brent at $110, USO +9%, and natgas fell 3% the same week. That is not a global energy shortage, that is a chokepoint trade. Different instrument, different risk: oil is paying for Hormuz insurance, gas is not.
items.tweetB: Energy +4.5%, staples +5.4%, tech -7.2%, semis -10.5%. A week where the defensive sectors outran the index by 7 to 15 points and S&P was only -1.95%. Index math hides how violent the rotation was.

items.title: CoreWeave -25% on the week, 5y CDS 1,117bp: a financing story wearing a macro costume
items.idea: CoreWeave lost a quarter of its value and its five-year default insurance widened to 1,117bp. HY spreads at the stress line, IG a few bp wider, widening concentrated in AI infrastructure. Dauber: two more HY prints above the line and the growth-scare call wins; Meta and Tesla calls on Wednesday are the next test.
items.angle: Single-name CDS at 1,117bp is distressed pricing on the poster child of GPU-backed debt. Watch whether hyperscaler capex guidance on Wednesday offsets it.
items.tweetA: CoreWeave 5y CDS at 1,117bp. That is not a growth-stock drawdown, that is the market pricing the GPU-collateralized debt stack as credit risk. Meta guides capex Wednesday. The neocloud balance sheet is the AI trade's weakest link.
items.tweetB: Everyone is asking if AI demand is real. The CDS market is asking a different question: who is still funded in 18 months. 1,117bp says the answer is not everyone.

items.title: Houthi pressure on KSA, Israeli elections next week, riots in France and India, midterms in 2 weeks
items.idea: Dauber's one-paragraph geopolitical risk stack: US midterms in two weeks with Democrats seen controlling at least one House; Houthi attacks causing political and economic damage to Saudi Arabia; Israeli elections next week that could change the government; massive riots ongoing in France and India.
items.angle: Four event risks stacked into the same fortnight as FOMC (27-28 Oct) and the Nov 4 refunding. Vol was under-hedged into CPI; this calendar is denser.
items.tweetA: Two weeks: midterms, Israeli elections, FOMC, Treasury refunding, and Houthis leaning on Saudi Arabia while Hormuz ships get hit. VIX at 19.99 is pricing a normal month. This is not a normal month.
items.tweetB: Riots in France and India at the same time as a Gulf shipping crisis. Everyone prices the oil leg. Nobody prices what unrest in two of the largest consumer markets does to the demand leg.

items.title: Tech breadth snapped: 68 of 75 tech names closed lower Friday, S&P held up on Dow and energy
items.idea: S&P 500 -1.95% to 7,659.44, Nasdaq 100 proxy -5.52%, Russell proxy -3.05%, Dow ETF +0.58%. Sixty-eight of seventy-five technology names closed lower on Friday. VIX 19.99 from 14.84 (intraday high 22.31). Hedging demand returned after being under-hedged into CPI.
items.angle: Index -2% understates the single-factor damage. Equal-weight and value outperformed; the cap-weighted headline is the lie.
items.tweetA: 68 of 75 tech names red on Friday alone. S&P -1.95% on the week looks orderly because the Dow and energy carried it. Under the hood this was a one-factor crash.
items.tweetB: VIX went 14.84 to 19.99. Not a panic, Dauber says. I would say it is the first time in months someone paid for protection instead of selling it. That changes dealer gamma into the next print.

items.title: Next catalysts: two HY prints, Meta/Tesla Wednesday, FOMC 27-28 Oct; Dauber's week-ahead regime call
items.idea: Regime moved from 'soft landing with hike in back pocket' to 'inflation shock absorbed by the long end while AI financing resets equities.' December hike near consensus. Dauber marks last week: right on shape (PPI, credit, duration), wrong on location (banks and small caps predicted, semis and AI credit delivered).
items.angle: Useful forecasting-hygiene habit: publish the miss. The market delivered the same shock to a different asset than expected.
items.tweetA: Dauber marked his own last call: right shape, wrong location. Called the stress in banks and small caps, got semis and AI credit. Good reminder that macro shocks are easy to size and hard to place.
items.tweetB: December hike near consensus while the 10y yields 5.09% and falling. A hiking Fed into a bull-flattening curve is how you invert the 2s10s again.

items.source: IT Tech PL / Bitcoin Market Report
items.title: Bitcoin -2.45% vs Nasdaq -4.5%: BTC lost about half as much, with ETFs still selling
items.idea: BTC range $79,800-$84,352; weekly candle $81,723 (-2.45%), second red week. US spot BTC ETFs -$156.6M (second outflow week), worst day Wednesday CPI day -$261.5M led by FBTC and IBIT. On-chain: selling eased while new buyers stayed away. Last week's $82,800 weekly-close line is now 1.3% overhead.
items.angle: BTC held up because holders sold less, not because buyers arrived. Support is passive; fragile if the macro tape keeps worsening.
items.tweetA: Nasdaq -4.5%, Bitcoin -2.45%, ETFs net sellers both weeks. BTC outperformed without a marginal buyer. That is a market held up by nobody selling, not somebody buying.
items.tweetB: Bitcoin dipped under $80k for the first time since mid-September and was back above $82k the same day. When the dip buyer shows up within hours but ETF flows stay red, who is it? Not IBIT.

items.title: Altcoins fell 2-4x harder than BTC; BTC.D 60.66%, third weekly gain
items.idea: 7-day: BTC -1.79%, ETH -3.88%, BNB -3.74%, SOL -5.92%, XRP -7.45%, ADA -11.64%, HYPE -7.83%, DOGE -7.62%, Pump.fun -21.87% (after -13.52%). Monero +9.90% was the only strong large cap. TOTAL $2.70T (-3.57%), TOTAL2 $1.06T (-5.19%), OTHERS $219.49B (-8.86%). BTC.D +0.69pt to 60.66%.
items.angle: Classic risk-off ordering: size and liquidity win. The Monero outlier is a privacy bid in a week of macro stress.
items.tweetA: OTHERS -8.86%, TOTAL2 -5.19%, TOTAL -3.57%, BTC -1.8%. The further you go down the cap table, the worse the week. Dominance 60.66% and rising for three straight weeks. Alt season is a rounding error.
items.tweetB: The only large cap up this week was Monero, +9.9%. In a week where everything with a ticker sold off, the privacy coin caught a bid. Nobody is talking about it.

items.source: IT Tech PL / Bitcoin Market Report
items.title: AI Networking & Data Centers -22.4% and Bitcoin Miners -19.9% (5-day): miners now trade as AI infra
items.idea: Artemis 5-day sector view: AI Networking & Data Centers -22.4% (worst of 25 sectors), Bitcoin Miners -19.9% (second worst, bottom two for a third straight week). Many listed miners also host AI compute and fell with data-center stocks. Only four sectors were green, including Crude Oil & NatGas +5.0%.
items.angle: Miner-to-AI-host pivot imports AI financing risk into the BTC miner complex. Hashprice is now the secondary driver.
items.tweetA: Bitcoin miners -19.9%, AI networking and data centers -22.4%. Same week, same direction, same magnitude. The market no longer thinks of miners as a Bitcoin proxy. They are AI landlords with a crypto sideline.
items.tweetB: Miners pivoted to hosting AI compute to escape hashprice. This week they inherited the AI financing problem instead. Diversifying into a drawdown.

items.source: IT Tech PL / Bitcoin Market Report
items.title: Ether ETFs -$250M, ETH taker CVD sell-dominant for a third week, Coinbase premium negative all 168 hours
items.idea: Ether ETFs -$250.4M, Solana ETFs -$25.5M, XRP ETFs -$1.8M. CryptoQuant 90-day taker CVD on ETH futures reads Taker Sell Dominant for a third week while spot is neutral. Coinbase premium gap negative for all of the last 168 hours (one positive hour the prior week).
items.angle: US spot demand for ETH is absent: zero positive Coinbase-premium hours in a week. Futures leading, spot not confirming.
items.tweetA: ETH Coinbase premium negative for 168 out of 168 hours. Zero hours of US spot bid. ETH ETFs -$250M, more than BTC ETFs. The US allocator is not just absent, they are leaving.
items.tweetB: ETH futures are sell-dominant, spot is neutral. That mismatch resolves one of two ways: spot capitulates, or shorts get squeezed on a headline. Funding will tell you which.

items.source: IT Tech PL / Bitcoin Market Report
items.title: CPI 3.7% vs 3.6%, gasoline +9.1% m/m; Fed already hiked in Sept to 3.75-4.00%; Warsh: 'I don't prejudge meetings'
items.idea: Sept CPI +3.7% y/y (3.6% exp), core 2.6% (2.5%), gasoline +9.1% m/m made up more than half of the rise. PPI +1.3% m/m vs 0.5% exp. Fed raised to 3.75-4.00% in September; CME odds of an Oct 28 hike went ~50% post-CPI to ~28% by Thursday. 10y spiked to ~5.33% intraday, closed 5.19%, then 5.10% Thursday. Chair Kevin Warsh in Bangkok Friday gave no hint.
items.angle: Headline inflation is an energy story (gasoline), core is only 2.6%. A hike in that setup is a policy choice into a supply shock.
items.tweetA: Gasoline was more than half of the CPI increase. Core is 2.6%. The Fed has already hiked in September and the question is whether it hikes into an oil shock. Warsh: 'I don't prejudge meetings.' Translation: you prejudge it.
items.tweetB: Hike odds for Oct 28: 50% after CPI, 28% by Thursday. 10y: 5.33% intraday, 5.19% close, 5.10% Thursday. The market faded its own panic in 48 hours. What did the bond market learn that the CPI print did not tell it?

items.source: IT Tech PL / Bitcoin Market Report
items.title: Kospi -20% in seven sessions; chipmakers down eight days straight
items.idea: South Korea's Kospi fell 20% in seven sessions through Thursday. Chipmakers fell eight days in a row, giving the Nasdaq its worst week since June (-4.5% per this source).
items.angle: A 20% drawdown in a major index in seven sessions is a liquidation event, not a repricing. Memory/semis concentration in Korea transmitted the AI unwind.
items.tweetA: Kospi -20% in seven sessions. Chips down eight straight days. That is not a rotation, that is margin calls. Whoever was long Korean memory as the cleanest AI proxy just found out how crowded it was.
items.tweetB: Korea fell 20% in seven sessions and Topdown is calling it cheap after a major reset. Cheap is a valuation. The question is whether the forced sellers are done.

items.source: IT Tech PL / Bitcoin Market Report
items.title: Attacks on at least nine ships near Hormuz push Brent to $110, highest since May
items.idea: Attacks on at least nine ships near the Strait of Hormuz pushed Brent to $110 Friday, its highest since May. Crude Oil & NatGas was one of only four green crypto-sector baskets (+5.0%).
items.angle: Nine ships in a week is a shipping-insurance event. Combined with Houthi pressure on KSA it raises chokepoint risk on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula.
items.tweetA: Nine ships hit near Hormuz in one week. Brent $110. Equities down 2%, bonds bid. The market is treating this as a growth shock rather than a supply shock. That reading breaks the first time a tanker sinks.
items.tweetB: Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb pressured at once, per Dauber's Houthi note. Oil traders price one chokepoint at a time. Both at once is a different distribution.

items.title: VaR shock plus forced deleveraging: Qs -550bps, Dow +50bps; echoes July 'Situational Awareness blowup'
items.idea: Slightly hot CPI triggered a VaR shock: dollar and bonds got flight-to-safety bids, as did defensives; everything else sold together. Eliant sees forced deleveraging similar to July's Situational Awareness blowup. Qs lost just over 550bps on the week; Dow +50bps on continued Value-over-Growth rotation. Tech, momentum and growth were the worst factors.
items.angle: Reference to a July fund blowup as the precedent for the mechanics (forced deleveraging in crowded AI longs).
items.tweetA: Dow +50bps, Nasdaq -550bps in the same week. A 6-point spread. That is a factor liquidation, not a view on rates.
items.tweetB: Eliant compares this to July's Situational Awareness blowup. When two separate deleveraging events in four months hit the same crowded basket, the basket is the risk.

items.title: Only 28% of stocks above 50D and Fear-Greed in Extreme Fear with S&P just 230bps from ATH
items.idea: % above 20D rebounded to 40% (slightly oversold), % above 50D at 28% (firmly oversold, moving toward extreme). S&P sits 230bps below all-time highs yet Fear-Greed is in Extreme Fear. The Mag-7 'generals' finally got hit this week.
items.angle: Sentiment washout without price washout. Historically fear readings this extreme usually accompany deeper drawdowns than 2.3%.
items.tweetA: S&P 2.3% from ATH. Fear-Greed at Extreme Fear. 28% of stocks above their 50-day. The tape and the sentiment gauge disagree by about 8 points of drawdown. One of them is catching up.
items.tweetB: Breadth washed out before the index did. Historically that ordering produces the best entries. Or the index is about to catch down to breadth, which is what MktContext thinks.

charts.desc: Fear-Greed Index overlaid with S&P; STD channels on SPY/QQQ/IWM/DJIA

items.title: Eliant track record since June 2023: +200.4% vs QQQ +102.12%, 80.5% win rate
items.idea: Since June 2023: +200.4% from tactical trades/baskets vs QQQ +102.12%, SPY +84.08%, Dow +62.34%, small caps +55.41%. 80.5% win rate; average realized winner +27.13%, average loser -14.58%.
items.angle: Expectancy per realized trade ≈ 0.805×27.13 − 0.195×14.58 ≈ +19%. High win rate, loss/win ratio ~0.54.
items.tweetA: Eliant: 80.5% win rate, +27.1% avg winner, -14.6% avg loser. Expectancy about +19% per closed trade. The part nobody quotes: losers averaging half the size of winners is what makes an 80% hit rate worth anything.
items.tweetB: A Substack PM that beats QQQ by 2x over three years. The question is not alpha, it is how much of it was 2023-25 AI beta. This week the Q's lost 5.5%.

items.title: Newsletter PMs are becoming copy-trading platforms: Plutus auto-replicates a portfolio into your IBKR account
items.idea: Eliant joined Plutus (RunPlutus): link an IBKR brokerage and trades, position changes and rebalances are replicated automatically while the follower keeps custody. Positioned as access to an actively managed portfolio without fund structures or high minimums.
items.angle: Distribution of research is converging with distribution of execution. Substack PM -> auto-replicated account is a mini-RIA without the wrapper.
items.tweetA: Newsletter PM publishes a portfolio. Follower links IBKR. Trades replicate automatically, no fund structure, no minimum. The research-to-execution gap just closed for retail.
items.tweetB: This is the part of fintech I find underrated: custody stays with the broker, the strategy is a subscription. Fee compression for every long/short fund that charges 2 and 20 for beta.

items.title: Nasdaq/10y correlation flipped from negative to positive: bonds are hedging again
items.idea: PaperAlfa: correlation between Nasdaq and 10-year yields flipped from negative in mid-September to positive this week. Equities weakened, yields fell, and bonds protected despite the inflation upside surprise. Consistent with price action becoming more sensitive to growth and risk appetite.
items.angle: Positive stock-bond yield correlation = bonds as the hedge. After years of 60/40 failure that is a regime variable I can track.
items.tweetA: Nasdaq/10y-yield correlation flipped sign in about a month. When equities fall, yields fall. Bonds are a hedge again, right when everyone had given up on them. Cheapest portfolio insurance may be the one that just started working.
items.tweetB: Inflation surprised higher and bonds still hedged equities. If the correlation holds through the FOMC, duration is no longer the problem trade. It is the portfolio stabilizer.

items.title: 'Cost of capital': investors now separate AI demand from the economics of financing the buildout
items.idea: PaperAlfa frames AI as one of the most powerful US economic forces (growth, capex, rates). As cost of capital rises, investors are distinguishing extraordinary AI demand from the economics of financing infrastructure. A forthcoming post will tackle AI, credit, inflation and the Fed. Asset allocation model shifted after being on the sidelines since summer; 2026 buy-and-hold portfolio closing in on new highs.
items.angle: Same theme as Goldman/CoreWeave: the debate moved from 'is demand real' to 'who can fund it'. Allocation model re-engaging after a summer on the sidelines is a contrarian-ish signal.
items.tweetA: The AI question changed this week: not 'will it work' but 'who pays the interest'. Demand and financing are different risks and the market just started pricing them separately.
items.tweetB: A systematic allocation model that sat out since summer is moving back in while equities fall. Models like that buy weakness only after trend and breadth reset. That is a data point on how far the reset went.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman, Mark Wilson)
items.title: Goldman: AI unwind may be overshooting; hedge fund damage severe in Asia and TMT but no sign compute demand rolled over
items.idea: Mark Wilson (Goldman): after three months of AI trade moving backwards, this week looked like capitulation. Hedge fund damage is severe, especially Asia and TMT, but Goldman sees no convincing evidence compute demand or pricing has rolled over. Positioning and sentiment may now be overshooting fundamentals.
items.angle: Sell-side calling a capitulation low is a lagging indicator, but the specific claim (compute pricing intact) is checkable via GPU rental indices.
items.tweetA: Goldman sees capitulation in AI positioning and no evidence compute pricing has rolled. If that holds, this is a positioning crash, not a demand crash. Check GPU rental prices before you sell the next leg.
items.tweetB: Three months of AI trade moving backwards and the first sell-side call for a new leadership trade arrives on the first real capitulation week. Calls like this come when there is nothing left to sell, or just before the next leg.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman, Mark Wilson)
items.title: Next AI phase: separate the biggest self-funding spenders from the weaker parts of the financing chain
items.idea: Goldman: the next phase is less about chasing every AI beneficiary and more about separating the biggest self-funding spenders from weaker parts of the financing chain. CoreWeave still sits at the center of the bear case. Bonds have started to hedge again, which may matter as much as the AI positioning reset if yields exhausted their move.
items.angle: Pair framework: long self-funded hyperscalers vs short debt-funded neoclouds. CoreWeave CDS at 1,117bp (Dauber) is the cleanest hedge instrument.
items.tweetA: The AI trade splits in two. Companies that fund capex from cash flow and companies that fund it from the HY market. CDS at 1,117bp already knows which is which.
items.tweetB: Self-funding hyperscalers versus borrowed-GPU neoclouds. Same demand, opposite balance sheets. This is the pair trade the AI unwind makes obvious.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Citi, Jason Williams)
items.title: Citi: Treasury dealer questionnaire reads as groundwork to cut 20Y and 30Y auction sizes at Nov 4 refunding
items.idea: Jason Williams and Citi's rates team read Treasury's latest dealer questionnaire as consistent with cutting 20-year and 30-year auction sizes on November 4. Long end has been fighting poor demand, elevated yields and heavy competing issuance. Citi expects the burden to migrate to bills rather than disappear.
items.angle: Supply cut at the long end is a direct bullish term-premium catalyst and explains part of the long-bond rally Dauber wants to fade. Lands 6 days after the FOMC.
items.tweetA: Treasury looks ready to cut 20Y and 30Y auction sizes at the Nov 4 refunding. The long end is rallying on growth fear while Citi says it also has a supply catalyst. Dauber's fade into FOMC is fighting two bids.
items.tweetB: Cutting the long end means more bills. More bills means more money-market demand and a bigger funding-market footprint. Treasury is telling you it does not want to term out debt at 5.4%.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Citi, Jason Williams)
items.title: Treasury trimming long coupons shifts the burden to bills; funding problem intact
items.idea: Citi expects shifts in issuance composition to be friendlier to duration but the broader funding problem to remain: the burden migrates to bills. Timing coincides with the AI unwind making Treasuries a hedge again, so long end may move from problem child to portfolio stabilizer.
items.angle: Shorter weighted-average maturity of debt raises rollover sensitivity to the front end, where Dauber says a hike is priced (2y 4.74%).
items.tweetA: Fewer 30-year auctions, more bills. Treasury has a 5.43% long bond and a 4.74% 2-year. It is choosing to fund at the front. That makes every Fed hike a bigger direct fiscal cost.
items.tweetB: Long end calming from supply cuts while the Fed may hike at the front end. Steeper issuance in bills against flatter yield curve. The curve and the issuance mix are moving in opposite directions.

items.title: 10y fell to 5% (three-week low) yet stocks fell sharply; Nasdaq -~6%; failed breakout above ATH
items.idea: MktContext market timer: PAUSE. Market failed to sustain a break above all-time highs; broad index 'catching down' to weak breadth as the last leaders fall. 10y yield fell to a three-week low of 5%, but instead of rallying like they should, stocks fell. Nasdaq lost almost 6% on the week. Full AI-bubble analysis is paywalled.
items.angle: Nasdaq weekly loss is quoted differently across sources (4.5% IT Tech, 5.52% Dauber, ~5.5% Eliant, ~6% MktContext), which is worth noting when citing. Direction agrees.
items.tweetA: Bond yields fell to a three-week low and equities fell with them. For most of 2022-25 that combination meant good news for stocks. Now it means the bond market is the one pricing recession.
items.tweetB: Stocks failed to hold a break above ATH and the leaders are the last to fall. That is the standard late-stage breadth pattern. The only thing different this time is that bonds are bid.

items.title: Apple store lines for the 'Duo' and iPhone 18 Pro Max while commentary says 'Black Monday'
items.idea: Ben Pouladian: Apple was trading near $350 before Friday's open; he visited Apple stores and saw lines of people trying to buy the Duo, with those unable to get one buying the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Banks describe a resilient economy with consumers spending. He calls the anecdote not a forecast, but argues the doom narrative deserves more scrutiny.
items.angle: Store-line anecdotes are a weak signal but pair well with bank commentary. The consumer is not the problem in this sell-off; the capex financier is.
items.tweetA: Lines at the Apple store for a new Apple device while Twitter says Black Monday. Retail does not read macro. The sell-off is a leveraged-institution problem, not a consumer problem.
items.tweetB: Bank earnings say consumers are spending. Apple store lines say the same. The sell-off is a leverage and financing story. Those are different crises with different Fed responses.

items.title: Bear case checklist: higher rates, neocloud financing, token commoditization, lab revenue gap, Chinese memory supply, lower multiples
items.idea: Pouladian summarizes the bear case someone laid out: higher rates, neocloud financing concerns, token commoditization, lab revenues that still need to catch up with spend, Chinese memory supply, political/geopolitical risk, and stocks continuing to find lower multiples. He says these are legitimate; being right about AI over five years does not mean being right about every stock over ten weeks.
items.angle: Chinese memory supply is the one item I can't see in other sources: a supply-side threat to HBM/DRAM pricing and a link to Kospi -20%.
items.tweetA: Seven-item AI bear case: rates, neocloud financing, token commoditization, lab revenue gap, Chinese memory supply, politics, multiple compression. Notice that only one of the seven is about demand. Five are about price of money or price of output.
items.tweetB: Chinese memory supply as an AI bear factor, plus Kospi -20% in seven sessions. The market may be pricing a memory-price collapse before anyone has seen it in contract prices.

items.title: Lower inference costs can expand the market while still hurting individual providers
items.idea: The checklist Pouladian will use through year-end: are orders turning into revenue and cash flow? Are projects funded or dependent on another capital raise? Do cheaper tokens create enough extra paid usage? Are enterprises moving beyond pilots? Lower inference costs can expand the market while hurting providers; financing pressure can expose weak businesses without invalidating the infrastructure buildout. Heading to GTC Berlin to see what is deployed and who pays.
items.angle: Jevons-for-tokens framed as a provider-level risk, not a market-level one. Ties to Hybrid Reasoning Agents (3x cheaper) in this window's paper list.
items.tweetA: Token prices fall, usage rises. Market expands, individual providers get less per unit. Same math as airlines: great for passengers, unclear for shareholders. Own the buyers or the scarce input, not the commodity producer.
items.tweetB: Today's paper list shows agent harnesses cutting token use 35-55% and cost 2.7-3.7x. Cheaper tokens are arriving faster than the bear case assumes. Revenue per token is the number to watch.

items.title: Korean equities look cheap after a major reset, but macro headwinds and positioning unwind could run longer
items.idea: Callum Thomas: Korean equities are starting to look cheap after a major reset, yet macro headwinds remain and the downturn could go further for longer (positioning unwind, earnings uncertainty).
items.angle: Fits Kospi -20% in seven sessions. Cheap-after-reset is the early bottom-fisher's argument.
items.tweetA: Kospi down 20% in seven sessions and Topdown calls it cheap but not safe. Memory earnings uncertainty is what decides whether this is a buy or a trap.
items.tweetB: Cheap after a 20% crash is not a signal. Cheap with intact earnings is. Korea is a leveraged bet on the memory cycle, so the memory price is the whole thesis.

items.title: Still bullish US small caps: cheap valuations, contrarian sentiment, technical reset
items.idea: Thomas remains bullish small caps despite recent weakness: cheap valuations, contrarian bullish sentiment/positioning, and a reset in technicals. Expects stabilization/rebound soon. (Russell proxy -3.05% this week per Dauber.)
items.angle: Small caps fell 3.05% in a week with a hiking Fed and 5%+ long yields: that is the opposite of the usual rate-sensitive thesis. Thomas is betting on positioning over rates.
items.tweetA: Small caps -3% in a week of 5% 10-year yields and a Fed that may hike. Topdown is still bullish. The case rests on positioning, not rates. That is a high-conviction contrarian call.
items.tweetB: Small caps are the one equity group that benefits most if the long-end rally turns into a Nov 4 supply cut. Rate relief is the only catalyst they need.

items.title: Upside risk for commodities: constrained supply, thematic demand, messier-for-longer geopolitics
items.idea: Thomas sees upside risk for commodities given macro tailwinds, constrained supply, thematic demand drivers, 'messier for longer' geopolitics, and resurgent sentiment/positioning.
items.angle: Dauber has Brent at $109.86 and Maverick shows commodities Sharpe 0.04 since 1995. Positioning data from a macro-chart specialist is a useful check.
items.tweetA: Commodities Sharpe since 1995: 0.04, per Maverick. That is why every rally gets sold. The question for this one is whether supply constraint plus geopolitics makes this cycle structurally different.
items.tweetB: Brent $110, 'messier for longer' geopolitics, resurgent positioning. The bull case is easy. The ugly part is what happens to demand when oil is at $110 and the Fed is hiking.

items.title: Agri commodities: cheap valuations, soft capex, El Nino weather risk, bullish technicals
items.idea: Thomas continues to see upside in agri commodities as a group: cheap valuations, soft capex, improving sentiment, weather risk (El Nino), geopolitics and bullish technicals.
items.angle: El Nino is the physical driver; soft capex means supply response is slow. Agri was absent from every other source in this window.
items.tweetA: Agriculture: cheap, under-invested, El Nino building. Supply response needs a planting season. Nobody on my feed is talking about grains while everyone watches oil.
items.tweetB: Soft capex plus weather plus geopolitics. Food is the second-order effect of the Hormuz shipping story that no one is pricing yet. Fertilizer comes from the same Gulf.

items.title: Topdown somewhat optimistic on Bitcoin: improved technicals, skeptical sentiment, but overhead resistance
items.idea: Thomas is somewhat optimistic on Bitcoin given improved technicals and still-skeptical sentiment/positioning, but hesitant on mixed macro signals and lingering technical hurdles (overhead resistance).
items.angle: Skeptical sentiment is constructive. IT Tech PL shows ETF outflows and a break of $82,800; Topdown sees positioning as already washed out.
items.tweetA: Sentiment on Bitcoin is still skeptical, ETFs are still selling, and price held better than the Nasdaq. A market that does not fall when it should is usually the one to watch.
items.tweetB: Two reads on the same chart: IT Tech PL sees a break under $82,800, Topdown sees improved technicals. Resistance versus support, same level.

items.title: Quantum circuit discovery: Reed-Solomon decoder Toffoli count 5.1M -> 440k; modular inversion architecture improved
items.idea: Anthropic, Harvard and QuEra paired an LLM (OpenEvolve search, Claude Mythos 5 proposing designs) with a verifying evaluator. On seven of eight tasks the circuits use fewer Toffoli gates and qubits than best-known designs, cutting combined cost 4.1x to 39x. Reed-Solomon decoder: Toffoli count from 5.1M to 440,000. On the eighth task it found a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion using divsteps.
items.angle: Prime-field modular inversion is the expensive primitive in elliptic-curve arithmetic (ECDSA, secp256k1). Cheaper reversible inversion lowers qubit/Toffoli estimates for breaking ECC.
items.tweetA: LLM-driven search cut a quantum decoder from 5.1M to 440k Toffoli gates and improved reversible modular inversion. Modular inversion is the expensive step in elliptic-curve arithmetic. Bitcoin's signature scheme runs on exactly that. The cost curve for Q-day just moved.
items.tweetB: The authors say some apparent costs of quantum arithmetic reflect limits of existing constructions, not of the algorithms. Algorithm discovery by AI is compounding on hardware progress. Two exponentials multiply.

items.title: LongHarness: same model, OfficeQA Pro exact match 15.8% -> 60.2% by managing evidence as explicit state
items.idea: Shanghai AI Lab / Fudan: for corpora of 100M+ tokens, keeping evidence and conclusions as explicit state. With GLM-5.3-Flash, OfficeQA Pro V1 15.8% -> 60.2%, V2 4.4% -> 61.1%. Beats Claude Code by 12.0 points on V1 and Codex by 18.9 on V2. Gains come from the harness, backbone fixed.
items.angle: Harness engineering is a bigger lever than model choice at this stage; matters for where value accrues (scaffolding vs weights).
items.tweetA: Same model. 4.4% to 61.1% on a benchmark by changing the harness. If scaffolding is worth 15x on a document task, the moat is not the weights. It is whoever builds the harness.
items.tweetB: LongHarness (a small Flash-class model) beat Claude Code by 12 points on OfficeQA Pro. Model quality is becoming a commodity input. The orchestration layer is where the margin is.

items.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents: 35-55% fewer tokens, 1.8-2.6x faster, 2.7-3.7x cheaper by reasoning in latent space
items.idea: Stanford / Together AI: agents reason in latent space and switch to text only for tool calls or answers (HybridLink). Across 3 model scales and 11 benchmarks it improves 10.4% on average over frontier agents; 14B model beats the strongest agentic baseline by 17.4%. Tokens down 35.5-54.7%, speed up 1.8-2.6x, cost down 2.7-3.7x.
items.angle: Direct hit on token-commoditization bear case (BEP list). Fewer tokens per task = lower revenue per task for API providers unless volume offsets.
items.tweetA: Agents that think in latent space use up to 55% fewer tokens and cost 2.7-3.7x less. For API providers that is a 3x revenue-per-task haircut. For buyers it is a 3x cheaper workforce. Demand elasticity decides who wins.
items.tweetB: Visible chain-of-thought is a cost center the buyer pays for. Latent reasoning removes the bill and the audit trail. The inspectable part is also what regulators will ask for.

items.title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting: research agents improve when their history is periodically wiped
items.idea: UC Berkeley / Stanford / Bespoke Labs: agents plateau as history accumulates because they anchor on past attempts. Fix: periodically discard every agent's session and candidate history and restart from the best candidate. Up to 15% over parallel agents, 39% over a single agent at same budget. On Anthropic's VLIW kernel take-home: 1,077 cycles vs 1,172 (four parallel agents) vs 1,262 (one agent).
items.angle: Counterintuitive: more memory is worse for open-ended search. Parallels human anchoring bias.
items.tweetA: Giving AI research agents more memory made them worse. Wiping history and restarting from the best result beat both parallel agents and a single agent. 1,077 cycles vs 1,262. Forgetting is a feature.
items.tweetB: Anchoring on past attempts is a human trading flaw too. Every desk that keeps a trade journal and a view of last month's P&L is running the plateaued version.

items.title: Harness^2 and ReHarness: agent harnesses that improve themselves at test time and revise old lessons backward
items.idea: Harness^2 (Google Cloud AI / Northwestern): test-time contrastive Propose-Probe-Compose without a ground-truth verifier; gains up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 on JobBench, 11.8 on LAB; five parallel candidate edits add 2.9-3.9 points. A memory baseline (ReasoningBank) fell up to 6.6 points below base. ReHarness (MIT/Meta/Yale): backward revision rewrites retrieved reflections after each task, beating raw-context, memory and prompt-optimization baselines on 16 tasks and three backbones.
items.angle: Self-improving harness without a verifier is the missing piece for open-world agents; one-way memory can actively hurt (-6.6).
items.tweetA: Memory baseline made agents 6.6 points worse than no memory. Agent memory that only writes forward accumulates stale lessons. The fix is revision, not more storage.
items.tweetB: Two papers in one week where the agent edits its own scaffolding without ground truth. Recursive self-improvement is arriving as boring engineering, one harness tweak at a time.

items.title: Sakana's Agentic Scientist: pipeline helped write a paper accepted as a main-conference talk at ALIFE 2026
items.idea: Sakana AI's end-to-end distributed pipeline (task drafting, ideation, planning, sandboxed experiments, baselines/ablations, analysis, report) with a meta-controller that checks each stage against a rubric. A development version helped write an ALIFE 2026 main-conference paper after human verification. Ablations: scientific autonomy depends on the orchestration layer as much as the base model.
items.angle: Peer-reviewed acceptance is a threshold crossing for AI-assisted research. Orchestration > model again.
items.tweetA: An AI-assisted pipeline got a paper accepted as a main-conference talk. With human verification, yes. But the ablation says autonomy depends on the orchestration layer, not the base model. Scientific labor is being repackaged as software.
items.tweetB: Research output is a function of agents in parallel with a rubric. That is also what a sell-side shop is. Who is the first bank to run it on earnings notes?

items.title: GitSwarm (Meta): hundreds of agents in one Git repo solve 30/30 IMOProofBench-Advanced; ProgramBench 79.4% at 500 workers
items.idea: Meta Superintelligence Labs: asynchronous agents share one Git repository; each contribution is a commit citing earlier commits on any branch; no central planner. With GPT-5.5 Codex workers it solves all 30 IMOProofBench-Advanced problems in one run; ProgramBench 79.4% (500 workers) vs 73.1% (100) vs 65.1% (single agent). Later workers build on 94.7% of published contributions; 70.1% of failed research commits are cited by later accepted work.
items.angle: Scaling by agent count, not model size: 65.1 -> 73.1 -> 79.4. Failed experiments are reused 70% of the time.
items.tweetA: Hundreds of agents, one Git repo, no planner. 65% -> 79% on ProgramBench by adding workers. 70% of failed commits got cited by later successes. Version control is the AI-era lab notebook.
items.tweetB: Compute scales with worker count. 500 agents cost 500x tokens. If a coordination protocol beats a bigger model, the compute demand curve shifts toward inference-at-scale. That is a different semis mix.

items.title: LoGRA (NVIDIA): full-weight RL post-training with less memory than LoRA; 27B on one 8-GPU node
items.idea: NVIDIA: compresses each weight gradient to a low-rank sketch redrawn every step plus predicted-KL step control. At 1.5B: 7.2 GiB vs 13.2 GiB for rank-256 LoRA. At 7B: -45.7% memory per GPU with accuracy near dense Adam. Trains a 27B model 1,100+ steps on a single eight-GPU node where dense Adam runs out of memory.
items.angle: Cheaper RL post-training = smaller labs can do frontier-style tuning on one node; shifts HBM demand per run.
items.tweetA: Full-weight RL on a 27B model on one eight-GPU node. Dense Adam runs out of memory there. Memory efficiency in training is HBM demand deferred, not destroyed.
items.tweetB: LoRA was the poor man's fine-tune. LoGRA gives full-weight updates for half the memory. Post-training is moving from a few labs to every enterprise with one rack.

items.title: AutoEnvScaling (Microsoft): an agent builds RL environments from rollouts, 25x more valid envs at 75% lower cost
items.idea: Microsoft and collaborators let a proposer agent design RL environments in a terminal, studying the trained model's rollouts. Up to 25x higher share of valid environments at up to 75% lower cost per valid environment. With Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as proposer and solver, Terminal-Bench 2.1 rises from 41.1 to 53.3.
items.angle: Environment supply is the bottleneck for RL scaling; automating it removes a human-data dependency.
items.tweetA: RL needs environments the way pretraining needed text. A model built environments for itself and Terminal-Bench went 41.1 to 53.3. The scarce input just became synthetic.
items.tweetB: 25x more valid environments at 75% lower cost per environment. Data-labeling vendors sell environments today. This is an automated supplier of the same thing.

items.title: Substack as a business: 11.5K subs doubled this year, open rate 50% -> 40%, $200/yr locked, half annual half monthly
items.idea: Rupak Ghose: 11,500+ subscribers (double this year), ~17K followers across 48 US states and 132 countries; open rate fell from ~50% to ~40% as it grew; paid conversion at average Substack level; Bestsellers in Business Top 50. Annual $200 (committed to hold), monthly raised $20 -> $30; about half annual and half monthly. Plans fully-paywalled long slide decks and a monthly price rise early next year. Readers include CEOs/founders of large hedge funds and prop firms.
items.angle: Niche-vertical newsletter economics: ~$200 ARPU with half of paid on annual. Also shows how a specialized topic (hedge funds/prop) attracts an elite reader base.
items.tweetA: 11.5K subscribers, $200 a year. Open rate dropped from 50% to 40% as the list doubled. Growth costs engagement. A niche newsletter with a few thousand paying hedge fund readers is a better business than most startups.
items.tweetB: He is removing old fintech pieces to narrow the focus to hedge funds, prop trading and market infrastructure. Narrower beats broader when your readers are the buyers. Specialization is the moat.

items.title: Hedge fund / prop firm map: overlap growing, 'peak pod shop', systematic trading cubs, Quadrature/Marshall Wace/Squarepoint deep dives
items.idea: Ghose is focusing on three areas: hedge funds, proprietary trading firms, and capital markets infrastructure. Themes called out as early: divergence in multi-manager platform business models, and the increasing overlap between hedge funds and prop firms. Upcoming: peak pod shop, systematic trading cubs, deep dives on Quadrature, Marshall Wace, Squarepoint, Octus, Bloomberg. Recent: Taula September returns; IFR piece 'Prime brokerage and Asia power Big Three's markets businesses'.
items.angle: 'Peak pod shop' coming right after July's Situational Awareness blowup and this week's deleveraging. Multi-manager deleveraging is the mechanism behind the factor crash.
items.tweetA: Eliant blames forced deleveraging like July. Ghose is about to write 'peak pod shop'. Multi-manager platforms run the same factor book with hard stops. That is how a CPI beat becomes a 550bp Nasdaq week.
items.tweetB: Hedge funds and prop firms are converging. One has gross leverage and a PM payout, the other has a seat and a risk cap. The Asia prime brokerage boom is the plumbing under it.

items.title: Since 1925: TIPS Sharpe 0.39 beats equities at 0.38; S&P +10.54%/yr at 18.48% vol
items.idea: Maverick's 1925-2026 chart: S&P 500 +10.54% annualized at 18.48% vol, Sharpe 0.38; Commodities +7.0%/17.32% vol, Sharpe 0.20; TIPS +5.33%/4.62% vol, Sharpe 0.39; Treasuries +4.86%/4.28% vol, Sharpe 0.31. Equities turned $1,000 into roughly $24M (text garbled); TIPS $188,604; Treasuries $119,320; commodities $911,785.
items.angle: Long-run Sharpe is similar across equities and TIPS. TIPS data before 1997 is reconstructed, so caveat that comparison.
items.tweetA: Since 1925 TIPS Sharpe 0.39, equities 0.38. Same risk-adjusted return, one with 4.6% vol, the other 18.5%. Lever the TIPS and you get equities with a floor. Nobody talks about it because TIPS don't have a ticker people tweet about.
items.tweetB: A century of data: commodities 7.0% return for 17.3% vol, Sharpe 0.20. They are a hedge, not a return stream. Buy them when the shock is supply-side, which is now.

items.title: Since 1995: gold +8.03% at 16.59% vol, Sharpe 0.33; commodities +3.14%, Sharpe 0.04
items.angle: Gold beats broad commodities by 5 points a year since 1995; the gold fund was -0.18% this week (Dauber) while oil +9%, so gold is not the shock hedge here.
items.tweetA: Since 1995: gold $10,817, broad commodities $2,595 on the same $1,000. Gold earned 8.03% at 16.6% vol; commodities earned 3.14% at 16.6%. Same volatility, 2.5x the compounding. Not all hard assets are equal.
items.tweetB: This week oil +9%, gold -0.18%. In 2026 gold is not the inflation hedge, it's the monetary regime hedge. They respond to different shocks.

items.title: 27 bear markets since 1925, one every 3.7 years, average -35% over 289 days; bulls +112% over 988 days
items.idea: Since 1925: 27 bear markets (-20% or more) vs 16 NBER recessions; bear markets every 3.7 years, recessions every 6.3 (1.7x as frequent). Average bear: -35% over 289 days (9.6 months); average bull: +112% over 988 days (2.7 years); stocks rise 78% of the time. Over a 20-30 year horizon expect 6-10 bear markets, 2-4 of them big. Recession duration: 23 months pre-WWII avg, 10.3 months post-WWII.
items.angle: Base rate to anchor Nasdaq -5.5% weeks: bears are normal; a bear market needs -20% from peak, and Nasdaq is nowhere near that yet.
items.tweetA: 27 bear markets in 100 years, one every 3.7 years. Average bull lasts 988 days; average bear 289 days. We have been in this bull for how long? The base rate says we are statistically due for something. It doesn't say when.
items.tweetB: Bear markets happen 1.7x more often than recessions. The market bounces out of most of them without a recession. Don't confuse a drawdown for an economic break.

items.title: Since 1995 only 2000 and 2008 drawdowns came with recessions, and those took 7.2 and 5.5 years to recover
items.idea: Six drawdowns since 1995: 1998 (-19.3%, recovered 4.2 months), 2000 (-49.1%, 929 days to trough, 7.2 years to recover), 2008 (-56.8%, 5.5 years), 2018 (-20%, 7 months), 2020 (-33.9% in 33 days, 6 months), 2022 (-25.4%, 2 years). Only 2000-02 and 2007-09 coincided with NBER recessions and they took by far the longest to recover. 1998, 2018, 2022 happened without recession.
items.angle: The asymmetry: recession-linked bear markets take 5-7 years to recover; non-recession bears recover in months to 2 years. So the question is: recession or not?
items.tweetA: Six drawdowns since 1995. The two with recessions took 5.5 and 7.2 years to recover. The four without took 4 months to 2 years. Nasdaq is down 5.5% in a week. Recession or no recession decides which bear market this is.
items.tweetB: 2020 was -33.9% in 33 days, recovered in 6 months. 2000 was -49.1% over 929 days. Speed of the drop didn't predict depth. The cause did.

items.title: Maverick launches model portfolios: All-Weather, Core-Satellites, All-Equities and a thematic AI Hedge Portfolio
items.idea: Maverick Equity Research is launching Maverick Model Portfolios: MAWP (All-Weather), MCSP (Core-Satellites), MAEP (All-Equities) and possibly MAIHP (AI Hedge Portfolio). Argues execution is now cheap: no high minimums, no prime broker, no AUM fees, tax-efficient. Also references fund-manager lessons from living through a -56.8% GFC drawdown.
items.angle: An 'AI Hedge Portfolio' as a product in the week AI unwound -5.5%: demand for exactly that hedge exists.
items.tweetA: A newsletter is launching an 'AI Hedge Portfolio' as a product. The week Nasdaq loses 5.5% and chips fall eight days in a row. When the retail product catalog adds an AI hedge, retail is positioned for AI.
items.tweetB: Model portfolios as a subscription: no minimum, no prime broker, no AUM fee. Execution has been commoditized. The scarce asset is the investor's behavior during a -56% drawdown.

items.title: McKinsey 'Shapers and Founders': what sets Asia's owner-CEOs apart
items.idea: New McKinsey book (Gautam Kumra, Cheryl Lim, Joydeep Sengupta) on Asia's owner-CEOs. Distinctive traits: deep sense of mission and resilience; balancing long-term vision with acute focus on the present; disciplined approach to both transformative and incremental innovation. Video discussion of lessons for CEOs, investors and board directors in any market.
items.angle: Owner-CEO lens on Asian companies: relevant for Korea/Taiwan/India founder-led compounders; governance as alpha.
items.tweetA: McKinsey on Asia's owner-CEOs: mission, long-term vision with short-term focus, and both big and small innovation. Founder-led firms outcompeting professional managers is a pattern you can screen for.
items.tweetB: Kospi -20% in seven sessions. Founder-led chaebols and owner-CEO companies behave differently in a liquidation than professionally managed ones. Who actually owns what you're holding?
